doc.title: Chuck Findley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 6, 2023

title: Jerry Hey, section mates and Findley's start on records in L.A.
summary: Findley praises Jerry Hey's writing, recalls the busy 1970s sessions, moving to L.A. in 1969 and Ollie Mitchell launching his record career.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Well that’s a lovely compliment I must say, Monk. Well I’ll tell you that really goes back to like when we were recording the lovely Al Jarreau stuff and just a lot of ridiculous things. And Jerry was a wonderful trumpet player when he could play, but then he had an issue with his throat and he couldn’t play anymore so he just became a writer, which he was anyhow, and he became a fantastic commercial writer. But Jerry would always, he would play everything he wrote before he brought it to a session, and, to make sure everybody could play it, which was — and it was difficult. And he was, like I said, what a marvelous trumpet player Jerry was. So he would play it, so we knew that it was playable, not necessarily going to be easy — but we knew it was playable. And well if you’ve heard any of the things that Jerry’s ever written and the things that we played, you would know how difficult it was. But back in those days, like I said — well I didn’t say it yet to you, to the people, but we were very busy running from one date to another date and back and forth. Gary Grant was also involved with that sessions, in the trumpet section, the three of us. But now we’re talking about in the ‘70’s now, mid-‘70’s to ‘80’s and all that. But way before that I was playing, well the records for me started, really started when I came here to town in — I moved here in ’69 and in ’70 I was very, very busy. Ollie Mitchell was my guru and Ollie basically got me started into records. You know he just took me with him everywhere and I was working three sessions a day besides jingles and film calls and movies as well. But it was — my breakthrough was at A&M — as a soloist I’m getting at, Monk — is when they asked me — it was for the Carpenters and it was on the tune “Close to You” and I played that flugelhorn solo on “Close to You” and I double tracked it and everybody heard that and from then on I got called to do so many solos on records, commercial records, Monk. Not jazz records.
